section_summary: This section combines California Joint Immigration Committee material alleging Japanese influence through language schools, public-school textbooks, dual citizenship, and immigration advocacy with military-intelligence reports about a Japanese census and possible mobilization activity on the Pacific Coast. A second major group concerns alleged Japanese naval espionage, including the Toshio Miyazaki–Henry Thompson investigation and extensive correspondence, press coverage, and legal preparations in the John S. Farnsworth case. The section ends with the State Department’s response to a trial subpoena and a memorandum recording Farnsworth’s February 1937 plea of nolo contendere.

subfiles.title: The Japanese Language Schools: Criticized as a Menace to American Citizenship
subfiles.about: Criticizes Japanese-language schools in Hawaii and California as instruments for maintaining loyalty to Japan among American-born Japanese children.
subfiles.summary: The release argues that Japanese-language schools use Japanese teachers, textbooks, and imperial ideology to cultivate allegiance to Japan. It reviews legislative attempts to regulate the schools in Hawaii and California and warns that Japan may distribute national-defense material through them. It concludes that separate schooling hinders the development of dependable American citizens and suggests teaching Japanese within public schools instead.

subfiles.title: Department of State Far Eastern Affairs file sheet
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Records the departmental handling of material filed under the Japanese military-activities subject.
subfiles.summary: This nearly blank sheet consists of Department of State and Far Eastern Affairs headings, routing marks, and file numbers. It contains no substantive narrative.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of McClatchy’s August letter and enclosures
subfiles.about: Acknowledges California Joint Immigration Committee material on Japanese veterans, armed Japanese, and language schools.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck thanks McClatchy for his August 19–20 letter and its enclosures. He notes enactment of legislation concerning Japanese veterans and expresses interest in the committee’s items on armed Japanese, its methods, Japanese-language schools, and textbooks. He invites McClatchy to send further information.

subfiles.title: Request for answers to E. C. Work’s questions
subfiles.about: Forwards constituent and Navy Department letters questioning American treatment of Japanese military information gathering.
subfiles.summary: Representative Caldwell forwards letters from E. C. Work and the Navy Department. He asks Secretary Hull to answer Work’s remaining questions and to return both enclosures.

subfiles.title: E. C. Work letter on unequal protection of military secrets
subfiles.about: Complains that Japanese visitors allegedly receive access in the United States that Japan denies to American tourists.
subfiles.summary: Work contrasts restrictions imposed on Americans at U.S. naval stations and near Japanese shores with alleged freedom granted to Japanese officers photographing American ports. He further claims that Japanese military representatives are invited to demonstrations of secret weapons and asks Caldwell to explain the apparent disparity.

subfiles.title: Navy Department response to E. C. Work
subfiles.about: Responds to allegations concerning naval-station access, foreign photography, and disclosure of secret naval information.
subfiles.summary: Swanson states that properly identified U.S. citizens generally may visit naval stations during designated hours. He notes the absence of a federal statute prohibiting foreigners from photographing U.S. topography. He denies that the Navy discloses information whose release could prejudice national defense.

subfiles.title: State Department explanation of Japan’s Fortified Zone Law
subfiles.about: Corrects the claim that any American tourist carrying a camera within three miles of Japan is automatically arrested.
subfiles.summary: The Department says Work’s allegation appears to rest on misinformation. It quotes provisions of the Japanese Fortified Zone Law prohibiting unauthorized surveying, photography, sketching, recording, and overflight within designated defensive zones. The letter explains that violators are liable under the statute and returns Caldwell’s enclosures.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Hornbeck’s August 12 letter
subfiles.about: Reports that Hornbeck’s letter has been forwarded to McClatchy at Lake Tahoe.
subfiles.summary: Kaltenbach acknowledges receipt of Hornbeck’s August 12 letter. She states that it has been forwarded to McClatchy at Lake Tahoe and that he will probably respond shortly.

subfiles.title: Military Intelligence Division distribution sheet
subfiles.to: War, Navy, State, and Commerce Department offices
subfiles.about: Provides a standard interdepartmental distribution list for military-intelligence material.
subfiles.summary: The form lists War Department branches, the Office of Naval Intelligence, State Department regional divisions, and Commerce Department units. No substantive report or marked disposition is visible.

subfiles.title: Japanese American Citizens League Southern California census appeal
subfiles.about: Solicits census information from Issei and Nisei residents for JACL and Japanese consular reports.
subfiles.summary: The item reproduces a census form requesting names, addresses, sex, age, birthplace, citizenship, marital status, and occupation. It asks Japanese people not already contacted to submit the form to JACL headquarters, stating that this will help complete reports for the league and the Japanese consulate.

subfiles.title: Military Intelligence Division distribution sheet
subfiles.to: War, Navy, State, and Commerce Department offices
subfiles.about: Standard routing form associated with intelligence concerning the Japanese census.
subfiles.summary: This page repeats the Military Intelligence Division’s distribution list. It contains no narrative beyond circulation and disposition options.

subfiles.title: Report on the Japanese census of Pacific Coast residents
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, War Department
subfiles.about: Reports a Japanese census of Japanese-born Pacific Coast residents and raises the possibility of military significance.
subfiles.summary: Jones states that Japanese organizations have been conducting the first census in several years of Japanese-born residents on the Pacific Coast. Notices in the Japanese Daily News urged cooperation with census takers. The report says any connection with Japanese military operations remains conjectural.

subfiles.title: Japanese census totals for Southern California and neighboring states
subfiles.about: Publishes Issei and Nisei census totals for Los Angeles districts, Southern California counties, Arizona, and New Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The clipping announces completion of the JACL census drive and credits Kiyoshi Okura with reporting results. It lists Issei and Nisei totals for numerous Los Angeles-area districts and for counties across Southern California, followed by figures for Arizona and New Mexico. The reported nine-county Southern California total is 42,873.

subfiles.title: Military Intelligence Division distribution sheet
subfiles.to: War, Navy, State, and Commerce Department offices
subfiles.about: Routes intelligence material concerning Japanese consular activity.
subfiles.summary: This is another standard Military Intelligence Division circulation form. It identifies potential departmental recipients but records no substantive information.

subfiles.title: Report of requests for Japanese mobilization forms
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, War Department
subfiles.about: Relays a report that Japanese men requested mobilization forms at the Japanese consulate in Los Angeles.
subfiles.summary: A Department of Labor representative relayed P. J. Seery-Siryk’s claim that he overheard about six Japanese callers request mobilization forms during a short visit to the Los Angeles consulate. The report suggests the activity may be connected with the census of Japanese nationals reported earlier in December.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Puleston espionage memorandum
subfiles.from: State Department, Division of Far Eastern Affairs; Stanley K. Hornbeck
subfiles.about: Directs readers to a memorandum on Captain Puleston’s evidence concerning the Japanese naval attaché and intelligence practices.
subfiles.summary: The note cross-references another file containing evidence of espionage reported by Captain Puleston in connection with the Japanese naval attaché. It states that the memorandum also discusses the theory and practice of military and naval intelligence services.

subfiles.title: Fragmentary report on recruitment for Japanese military aviation
subfiles.from: Headquarters intelligence office at the Presidio of San Francisco
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, War Department
subfiles.about: Reports an apparent effort to recruit a qualified American-born Japanese aviator for Japanese military flying service.
subfiles.summary: The surviving fragment says that an effort appears to have been made to obtain a qualified American-born Japanese for Japanese military aviation. It begins describing a fruit-market worker who had completed flying training and was approached by a Japanese officer, but the account is truncated.

subfiles.title: Despatch on a possible sighting of Toshio Miyazaki in Toronto
subfiles.from: Damon C. Woods, American consul at Toronto
subfiles.about: Reports a Toronto resident’s suspicion that a guest named T. Miyauchi might be espionage suspect Toshio Miyazaki.
subfiles.summary: Edward Patterson told Woods that a Japanese guest named T. Miyauchi had stayed at his tourist house and described his travels and stated interest in the textile industry. Patterson thought the man might be Toshio Miyazaki, then under indictment at Los Angeles. Woods considered the identification too indefinite for immediate police action but offered to seek Canadian assistance if Justice found the lead credible and the offense extraditable.

subfiles.title: Jap Spy Bureau in American Navy
subfiles.from: United Press; Toronto Mail and Empire
subfiles.about: Reports the indictment of Henry Thomas Thompson and Toshio Miyazaki for an alleged Japanese naval espionage conspiracy.
subfiles.summary: The article alleges that a paid spy ring obtained U.S. fleet gunnery and aviation information during Pacific maneuvers. It identifies former Navy yeoman Henry Thomas Thompson and Japanese naval officer Toshio Miyazaki as defendants and describes Miyazaki as the ring’s paymaster. The story says Miyazaki fled to Japan and that investigators had delayed action while seeking stronger proof.

subfiles.title: Forwarding the Toronto Miyazaki despatch to the attorney general
subfiles.about: Sends the attorney general a consular lead concerning a person who might be Toshio Miyazaki.
subfiles.summary: Hull encloses the June 25 Toronto despatch concerning a Japanese individual who might be the indicted Miyazaki. He acknowledges that little connects the person to the Los Angeles defendant but submits the information for whatever value it may have.

subfiles.title: Attorney General’s response on extradition
subfiles.about: Explains that no Canadian inquiry is needed because conspiracy is not extraditable under the applicable treaties.
subfiles.summary: Cummings acknowledges Hull’s transmission of the Toronto despatch. He states that conspiracy is not an extraditable offense under treaties between the United States and Great Britain and therefore no further action by the consul is necessary.

subfiles.title: Instructions to Consul Woods to take no further action
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore, for the secretary of state
subfiles.about: Notifies the Toronto consul that the Justice Department does not require an inquiry into T. Miyauchi.
subfiles.summary: Moore advises Woods that the State Department sent his despatch to the Department of Justice. Quoting the attorney general’s response, he explains that conspiracy is not extraditable under U.S.–British treaties and that the consul need take no further action.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Japanese Embassy note on Tamon Yamaguchi
subfiles.about: Points to a certified Japanese Embassy note concerning the arrival of naval attaché Tamon Yamaguchi for use in the Thompson case.
subfiles.summary: The note cross-references a certified copy of a Japanese Embassy communication concerning Captain Tamon Yamaguchi’s arrival. The Justice Department wanted the material for use in the Thompson espionage prosecution.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on pressure against a Harbin consular clerk
subfiles.about: References confidential reporting about Soviet and Japanese secret-authority pressure on an American consular clerk in Harbin.
subfiles.summary: The sheet directs readers to another file concerning pressure placed on E. S. Dresser, a clerk at the American Consulate General in Harbin. Both Soviet and Japanese secret authorities are identified as involved.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Japanese aeronautical engineers traveling to the United States
subfiles.from: American consular office at Nagoya; Stephan
subfiles.about: Records travel plans of two Japanese engineers visiting American aircraft concerns and studying aeronautical engineering.
subfiles.summary: The note identifies Minoru Nakao and Zenji Watanabe as representatives of Aichi Tokei Denki K.K. Nakao planned to visit aircraft factories and engineering concerns, while Watanabe was to undertake a ten-month aeronautical-engineering course at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Both received section 3(1) visas.

subfiles.title: Telephone memorandum on Senator Lonergan and the Farnsworth case
subfiles.about: Records Senator Lonergan’s demand that Japan repudiate an officer’s alleged corruption of an American for military information.
subfiles.summary: Lonergan telephoned about the Japanese spy case, apparently the Farnsworth matter, and asked what the State Department was doing. He said he and congressional colleagues believed Japan should publicly repudiate the alleged conduct of a Japanese government officer. Turner replied that he did not know the facts but would record the senator’s views.

subfiles.title: John S. Farnsworth’s confidential appeal to the secretary of state
subfiles.about: Argues that Japanese Embassy personnel could exonerate him and accuses officials and the press of sacrificing him to diplomatic convenience.
subfiles.summary: Farnsworth claims that four Japanese Embassy staff members in Washington could testify that he acted merely as an adviser and did not traffic in secret documents. He questions why the indictment instead names two officers already in Japan and suggests that officials wish to avoid a diplomatic uproar. He blames Hearst publicity and anti-Japanese agitation, asks the State Department to confer with him, and reserves the right to publicize his letter in self-defense.

subfiles.title: State Department reply disclaiming jurisdiction over Farnsworth’s case
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore, for the secretary of state
subfiles.about: Tells Farnsworth that his prosecution belongs to the Department of Justice, not the State Department.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges Farnsworth’s August 18 letter but rejects his assertion that it has taken official cognizance of the case through press statements. Moore states that the matter falls within Justice Department jurisdiction.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Farnsworth correspondence to the attorney general
subfiles.about: Forwards Farnsworth’s August 18 letter and the State Department’s acknowledgment to the attorney general.
subfiles.summary: The assistant secretary encloses copies of Farnsworth’s letter to the secretary of state and the Department’s reply. The short communication places the correspondence before the Justice Department.

subfiles.title: Handwritten Assistant Secretary routing note
subfiles.to: State Department official, probably Stanley K. Hornbeck
subfiles.about: A largely illegible note appears to request attachment of earlier correspondence.
subfiles.summary: The handwritten page is badly obscured by OCR. It appears to mention previous correspondence and direct that papers be attached for review.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs covering memorandum on McClatchy enclosures
subfiles.about: Recommends no comment on three anti-propaganda papers submitted by McClatchy.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum identifies an excerpt from Pacific Relations, Facts Which Walter Hoffman Overlooked, and Dangers Created by Japanese Dual Citizenship. It says the reviewing official probably will not wish to comment and notes that copies of the McClatchy–Field correspondence are also included.

subfiles.title: McClatchy letter enclosing criticism of Pacific Relations
subfiles.about: Sends material accusing Walter G. Hoffman’s textbook of serving Japanese propaganda objectives.
subfiles.summary: McClatchy encloses a statement and exhibits filed with California’s superintendent of public instruction concerning Hoffman’s Pacific Relations. He says the book could disseminate Japanese propaganda if used under instructors sharing Hoffman’s views. He presents the matter as evidence of a Japanese plan to influence American public schools.

subfiles.title: A Criticism of Pacific Relations—Hoffman
subfiles.from: V. S. McClatchy and the California Joint Immigration Committee
subfiles.about: Urges California to reject Hoffman’s textbook as a misleading presentation of Japanese immigration and policy.
subfiles.summary: The committee claims Hoffman’s chapter on Japanese immigration omits facts supporting U.S. exclusion policy and parallels a previously withdrawn Hawaiian text. It alleges cooperation among Japanese cultural organizations, educators, and the Institute of Pacific Relations in producing favorable teaching materials. The statement asks that misleading textbooks and the agencies responsible for them be excluded from public-school curricula.

subfiles.title: McClatchy reply to Frederick V. Field
subfiles.about: Defends public criticism of Institute of Pacific Relations educational projects against Field’s complaint.
subfiles.summary: McClatchy welcomes Field’s acknowledgment that the Hawaiian materials mishandled the Gentlemen’s Agreement and Japanese policy but rejects the charge that the committee publicized its concerns too broadly. He recounts earlier protests, alleged Japanese plans to influence American schools, and the Institute’s failure to respond promptly. He argues that public exposure was necessary to protect immigration law and school curricula from foreign propaganda.

subfiles.title: Field letter acknowledging errors in IPR school materials
subfiles.about: Acknowledges errors in Hawaiian teaching materials while criticizing McClatchy’s public campaign against the Institute of Pacific Relations.
subfiles.summary: Field concedes that the Hawaiian text contained erroneous references to the Gentlemen’s Agreement and other doubtful interpretations. He says the Japan and China units were abandoned and that an attempted collaboration with Japan’s Society for International Cultural Relations had proved unworkable. While thanking McClatchy for corrections, he objects to attacks on IPR projects before the organization had been given an opportunity to respond.

subfiles.title: Excerpt from Pacific Relations on Japanese emigration
subfiles.about: Presents a brief account of Japanese immigration to the United States and its effect on Pacific relations.
subfiles.summary: The poorly reproduced excerpt discusses population pressure in Japan, Japanese migration to the United States, exclusion legislation, and the continuing diplomatic dispute. It suggests the situation is unpleasant and should be resolved, language that the California committee regarded as overly sympathetic to Japan.

subfiles.title: Facts Which Author Walter Hoffman Overlooked
subfiles.from: V. S. McClatchy and the California Joint Immigration Committee
subfiles.about: Supplies the committee’s rebuttal to Hoffman’s account of Japanese immigration and the Gentlemen’s Agreement.
subfiles.summary: The paper argues that Japan violated the Gentlemen’s Agreement by permitting labor migration and population growth. It defends the 1924 exclusion provisions as nondiscriminatory and necessary to prevent broader Asian immigration. It also contends that Japan applies comparable restrictions within its own sphere and should withdraw demands for a U.S. quota.

subfiles.title: Dangers Created by Japanese Dual Citizenship
subfiles.about: Argues that retention of Japanese nationality by American-born Japanese creates divided loyalty in Hawaii and California.
subfiles.summary: The paper reviews Japan’s 1924 nationality law and contends that family influence, language schools, and cultural education discourage expatriation. Using figures supplied by Governor Joseph Poindexter, it claims that two-thirds of eligible Hawaiian-born Japanese retained Japanese citizenship. It warns that similar conditions probably existed in California and criticizes the inclusion of Japan-raised Kibei within the Japanese American Citizens League.

subfiles.title: Why Immigration Quota Should Not Be Granted to Japan
subfiles.from: V. S. McClatchy and the California Joint Immigration Committee
subfiles.about: Sets out historical and racial arguments against granting Japan an immigration quota.
subfiles.summary: McClatchy traces U.S. citizenship and exclusion policy and argues that the Gentlemen’s Agreement failed because Japan violated it. He says any Japanese quota would undermine the 1924 exclusion principle and require similar concessions to other Asian peoples. The pamphlet also invokes alleged racial incompatibility, dual citizenship, and the risk of renewed friction in California.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of McClatchy’s Pacific Relations material
subfiles.about: Thanks McClatchy for his letter and enclosures criticizing Hoffman’s Pacific Relations textbook.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck acknowledges McClatchy’s letter written at Tahoe City and San Francisco. He expresses appreciation for the information about Hoffman’s textbook and its accompanying materials.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Bull’s allegations about Farnsworth
subfiles.about: Records Bull’s assertion that Farnsworth had spied for Japan and might be mentally ill.
subfiles.summary: Bull claimed Farnsworth had engaged in espionage for at least two years and had admitted being a Japanese spy while negotiating to sell his story to a newspaper syndicate. He said the material reached Naval Intelligence and J. Edgar Hoover, after which Farnsworth was placed under surveillance. Bull warned that a trial could implicate senior Japanese officials and recommended private psychiatric commitment as a quieter means of investigating Farnsworth’s claims.

subfiles.title: Farnsworth Asks Japanese to Aid Him Clear Self
subfiles.about: Reports Farnsworth’s requests for affidavits from five Japanese naval officers.
subfiles.summary: Farnsworth sought statements from Tamon Yamaguchi, B. Yamaguchi, Jo, Yoshiyuki Itimiya, and Okira Yamaki that his relations with the Japanese Navy were legitimate advisory work. The article quotes him as saying he received expenses and variable bonuses and expected eventually to assist aviation reorganization in Japan. It also reports his pending arraignment and his parallel appeal to the State Department.

subfiles.title: Japanese Aids Reject Appeal by Farnsworth, first clipping
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese naval attaché Tamon Yamaguchi’s refusal to provide Farnsworth with an affidavit.
subfiles.summary: The article says Farnsworth asked five Japanese officers to attest that his advisory relationship with the Japanese Navy was legitimate. Tamon Yamaguchi denied knowing Farnsworth and stated that he could not supply an affidavit. The clipping also notes the attaché’s expected departure for Japan and Farnsworth’s pending prosecution.

subfiles.title: Japanese Aids Reject Appeal by Farnsworth, duplicate clipping
subfiles.about: A second copy of the report that Japanese officials rejected Farnsworth’s request for affidavits.
subfiles.summary: This duplicate repeats that Farnsworth sought statements from Japanese naval officers to support his defense. Tamon Yamaguchi denied knowing him and refused to assist. The surviving copy ends during its description of the conspiracy indictment.

subfiles.title: Japan Watches U.S. Elections With View to Trade Agreement
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese plans to pursue a bilateral trade commission after the U.S. presidential election.
subfiles.summary: The story says Japan wanted improved commercial relations but believed the American election had delayed negotiations. It reviews bilateral trade figures and Japanese objections to higher U.S. duties and taxes on several products. Japanese authorities expected Commercial Counsellor Inouye to report American views on a permanent commission.

subfiles.title: Continuance for Farnsworth defense demurrers
subfiles.about: Announces a two-week extension for filing defense papers in the Farnsworth espionage case.
subfiles.summary: District Attorney Leslie C. Garnett granted Farnsworth’s counsel additional time to study recent developments. Attorney William E. Leahy was given until September 22 to file defense demurrers.

subfiles.title: McClatchy letter on investigation of school propaganda
subfiles.about: Reports publicity and a prospective California Board of Education investigation into alleged Japanese propaganda.
subfiles.summary: McClatchy thanks Hornbeck for suggestions and encloses committee release number 456. He says California newspapers have publicized the textbook issue and expects the State Board of Education to appoint experts to investigate. He notes that complete sets of the committee’s evidence are available in Washington offices.

subfiles.title: Japanese Propaganda in the Public Schools
subfiles.about: Summarizes the committee’s charges against Hoffman’s textbook and Japanese cultural influence in American schools.
subfiles.summary: The release claims Hoffman’s Pacific Relations conceals facts about Japanese immigration and fits a Japanese plan to cultivate American sympathy through education. It reviews protests in Hawaii and California and quotes alleged Japanese official statements about systematic school propaganda. It also recounts the preparation and later withdrawal of a Hawaiian text produced with Institute of Pacific Relations participation.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck letter suggesting wider distribution of McClatchy material
subfiles.about: Praises McClatchy’s response to Field and suggests sending relevant materials to other federal bodies.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck thanks McClatchy for his August 1 letter and enclosures, especially the exchange with Frederick V. Field. He considers McClatchy’s defense of his publicity campaign persuasive and suggests sending the correspondence to the Department of the Interior. He also asks whether dual-citizenship materials have been given to the interdepartmental committee reviewing U.S. nationality laws.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck acknowledgment of release on public-school propaganda
subfiles.about: Acknowledges McClatchy’s August 27 letter and enclosure on Japanese propaganda in public schools.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck states that he has returned from vacation and hastens to acknowledge the material. He thanks McClatchy for supplying the information.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to letters rogatory in United States v. John Semer Farnsworth
subfiles.from: Department of Justice, Office of the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia
subfiles.about: References interrogatories intended for Japanese naval officers in the Farnsworth prosecution.
subfiles.summary: The note points to letters rogatory in United States v. John Semer Farnsworth. It says the enclosed interrogatories were to be administered to members of the Japanese Navy and asks whether Japanese practice would permit the officers to answer them.

subfiles.title: Request for State Department records for the Farnsworth trial
subfiles.from: Leslie C. Garnett, U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia
subfiles.about: Requests documentary State Department evidence pursuant to a subpoena duces tecum for the Farnsworth trial.
subfiles.summary: Garnett says Farnsworth’s Espionage Act trial is set for February 15, 1937. Because the prosecution expects to introduce evidence that Farnsworth supplied Navy information to Japanese government agents, it requires documents held by State Department officers. Garnett asks Hull to ensure compliance with the subpoena directed to the chief clerk.

subfiles.title: State Department arrangements for inspection of subpoenaed records
subfiles.from: Department of State, for the secretary of state
subfiles.about: Invites the assistant district attorney to inspect assembled State Department records before their production at trial.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges Garnett’s letter concerning the subpoena in United States v. John S. Farnsworth. It reports that Assistant District Attorney Beach intends to call at the Department and says an inspection is desirable because the subpoena describes the evidence broadly. The assembled documents are held in Assistant Legal Adviser Baker’s office.

subfiles.title: Closure of subpoena matter after Farnsworth’s nolo contendere plea
subfiles.about: Records that State Department documents need not be produced because Farnsworth pleaded nolo contendere.
subfiles.summary: The writer recounts consultations with Assistant District Attorney Beach and a Justice Department representative concerning the requested records. Officials had agreed to identify the exact documents needed before trial. When Farnsworth pleaded nolo contendere on February 15, the case closed without production of the records.
